```{r setup, include=FALSE}
  echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center",

)

# Every number in this deck is read from the CSVs the targets pipeline writes
# (bsz-analysis/_targets.R: site_tab5_csv, site_inputs_csv,
# site_grid_csv, site_leavers_csv). Nothing below is retyped.
t5  <- read.csv("../data/tab5.csv")
ins <- read.csv("../data/inputs.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grd <- read.csv("../data/grid.csv")
lv  <- read.csv("../data/leavers.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tst <- read.csv("../data/test-results.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
W0 <- t5$wealth[1]; n0 <- t5$n_billionaires[1]
C  <- -t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[1] / 0.05
a  <- t5$avoidance_rate[1]; m <- 0.5   # alpha and the movers' share of it (inputs.csv)
stopifnot(abs(a - 0.10) < 1e-9, abs(-a * m * C - t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[1]) < 1e-9)
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
par <- read.csv("../data/pareto.csv"); ps <- read.csv("../data/pareto-summary.csv")
a_s <- 0.20                       # avoidance for the added, less visible fortunes (inputs.csv)
dW  <- t5$wealth[2] - W0          # wealth row 2 adds to the 1 July base
add_tax <- 0.05 * (1 - a_s) * dW; phase <- 0.025 * ps$fraction_in_phasein * dW
stopifnot(abs(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] + add_tax - phase - t5$wealth_tax_revenue[2]) < 1e-6)
bn <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
row1 <- with(grd, avoidance == 0.10 & mobility_share == 0.5 & avoidance_small == 0.2 &
                  abs(sell_share - 1/3) < 1e-9 & pareto == 0 & leavers == 0)
```

name: study-brief

# The study in brief

Boll, Saez and Zucman (NBER WP 35218, May 2026, revised August 2026) document the wealth of
California's billionaires, the taxes they pay, and what a one-time tax on them would raise.

- **Wealth.** California billionaires held **$2.3 trillion** by mid-2026, as much as all the
  income on all Californians' tax returns. Up 144% from 2023 to 2025, driven by the AI boom.
  Since 1982 the real wealth of the top 0.001% has multiplied by 25; average real family income
  has doubled.
- **Taxes.** They pay about **0.2% of their wealth** a year in California income tax
  ($3.2 billion a year), 2.4% of the state's income tax revenue over 2023 to 2025.
- **The top four.** SEC filings for Page, Brin, Zuckerberg and Huang (Ellison through 2020)
  show nearly $1 trillion in business wealth, about 40% of the total, taxed at 0.04% of wealth
  a year.
- **The proposal.** A one-off 5% tax, payable over five years, is small next to recent wealth
  gains and large next to taxes now paid. The authors estimate **about $100 billion**
  (Table 5: $`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion), with minor effects on income tax.

.small[The figures above are the paper's own, from its abstract. Every number from the Deck Map
onward is recomputed by the reproduction pipeline.]

# What is an Open Policy Analysis?

.opa-intro[
A policy analysis is **open** when a reader can see the one estimate it recommends, follow
every step from the inputs to that estimate, and rerun it. The
[Open Policy Analysis](https://tinyurl.com/1qypbihb) framework asks for three layers.
]

<img src="../assets/opa/opa-details.png" class="opa-mark" alt="">

.opa-legend[
**1. Open Output**: [the explorer](../explorer/), one preferred estimate, the assumptions as dials<br>
**2. Open Analysis**: [the report](../repro.html) and **this deck**, the chain from the Forbes
list to the revenue, step by step, with the guesswork marked<br>
**3. Open Materials**: [the repository](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/tree/main/bsz-analysis),
the pipeline, its tests and every exported CSV
]

name: part-policy
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 1: What is being estimated

---

# The tax, in one line

.pull-left[
**Proposition 40** (the Billionaire Tax Act):

- a **one-time** 5% tax on net worth
- on California residents on **1 January 2026**
- paid 1% a year over **five years**
- wealth valued on 31 December 2026

Directly held real estate is excluded; business real estate is not.
]

.pull-right[
**Two documents make the BSZ side's case**

1. Boll, Saez and Zucman (**BSZ**), NBER WP 35218, August 2026, with a public Excel
   workbook. Base scenario: **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion.**
2. Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske (**GGSS**), expert report, 20 July 2026:
   **$100 billion**.

.highlight-box[
GGSS p.4: "a scoring of $104 billion that we round to $100 billion for simplicity."
**The two are one computation.**
]
]

---
name: part-steps
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 2: Five steps to $`r round(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion

---

# Steps 1 and 2: Taxable base and evasion

**Step 1.** Forbes' real-time list on 1 July 2026: $n_0$ = `r n0` California billionaires
holding $W_0$ = $`r bn(W0, 0)` billion. **Data**, read off Forbes that day.

**Step 2.** Some wealth escapes: under-valued, hidden, or moved out in time. The authors
assume a share $\alpha$ = 10% of all of it together:

$$W^{\text{tax}} = (1-\alpha)\,W_0 = 0.9 \times `r bn(W0, 0)` = `r bn(t5$taxable_wealth[1])`$$

.highlight-box[
The 10% is <span class="guess">guesswork</span>. GGSS argue it is small: most of the wealth is
listed stock, easy to value, and 250 taxpayers can each be audited. Nobody has measured it,
because the tax has never existed.
]

.small[Details: [report, step 2](../repro.html#step-2-avoidance-and-evasion).]

---

# Step 3: the revenue

$$T = \tau \, W^{\text{tax}} = 0.05 \times `r bn(t5$taxable_wealth[1])` = `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])`$$

That is the whole headline: **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion, once**, paid in five
yearly installments of about $`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] / 5)` billion.

```{r fig-waterfall, fig.height=3.2}
d <- data.frame(
  step = factor(c("5% of the list", "less 10% avoidance", "revenue"),
                levels = c("5% of the list", "less 10% avoidance", "revenue")),
  value = c(0.05 * W0, -(0.05 * W0 - t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1]), t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1]))
d$start <- c(0, 0.05 * W0, 0); d$end <- d$start + d$value
ggplot(d, aes(x = step, xmin = as.numeric(step) - 0.35, xmax = as.numeric(step) + 0.35,
              ymin = start, ymax = end, fill = step)) +
  geom_rect() +
  geom_text(aes(y = pmax(start, end), label = paste0("$", bn(abs(value)), "B")), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#9aa6b2", "#e65100", "#1f6fce"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "$ billion")
```

---
name: step-4

# Step 4: selling assets to pay raises income tax

Some billionaires will sell stock to pay the tax. The authors assume a share $s$ = 1/3 of the
tax is paid by selling.

Not all of a sale is income. Only the **gain** is taxed: the sale price minus what the stock
originally cost (its **basis**). The authors put the gain at $g$ = 80% of each dollar sold, so the
basis is the other 20%. Example: selling $100 of stock bought for $20 gives an $80 taxable gain.

That gain is taxed at the top California rate on gains, $t_{cg}$ = 13.3%:

$$E = s \cdot g \cdot t_{cg} \cdot T = \tfrac13 \times 0.8 \times 0.133 \times `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` = `r bn(t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales[1], 2)`$$

.small[*E* is extra income tax, collected **once**, while the wealth tax is being paid.]

---
name: step-5-who

# Step 5, part 1: who leaves

Step 2 took a share $\alpha$ = `r pct(a)` of the wealth out of the wealth tax. In dollars:
`r pct(a)` of $`r bn(W0, 0)` billion is **$`r bn(a * W0, 2)` billion**.

That `r pct(a)` mixes two behaviours. The authors split it in half, $m$ = `r pct(m)`:

| Part of the escaped wealth | Share of all wealth | Wealth, $B | Still a CA resident? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Under-valued or hidden | $\alpha (1-m)$ = `r pct(a * (1 - m))` | `r bn(a * (1 - m) * W0, 2)` | yes |
| Owner **moves out** of California | $\alpha \, m$ = `r pct(a * m)` | `r bn(a * m * W0, 2)` | **no** |

.highlight-box[
Step 2 already removed **both** rows from the **wealth tax**. Step 5 asks about a different tax,
the **income tax**. Only the second row matters for it: people who still live in California keep
paying California income tax; people who moved out stop.
]

---
name: step-5-loss

# Step 5, part 2: the income tax they take with them

Today California billionaires pay $C$ = $`r bn(C, 2)` billion a year in California income tax.
That is about $`r bn(1000 * C / W0, 2)` of income tax for every $1,000 of wealth they hold.

The movers from the previous slide hold $`r bn(a * m * W0, 2)` billion. The authors assume they pay
income tax at that same rate, so their income tax is the same `r pct(a * m)` share:

| | Wealth, $B | Income tax, $B a year |
|---|---:|---:|
| All California billionaires | `r bn(W0, 0)` | `r bn(C, 3)` |
| The movers (`r pct(a * m)` of the wealth, $\alpha \, m$) | `r bn(a * m * W0, 2)` | `r bn(a * m * C, 3)` |

Once they leave, California loses that income tax every year:

$$L = -\alpha \, m \, C = -`r bn(a, 2)` \times `r m` \times `r bn(C, 2)` = -`r bn(-t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[1], 3)` \text{ per year}$$

.highlight-box[
The minus sign means revenue lost. $L$ is **per year**, and Table 5 does not say for how many
years. BSZ argue about 5; the [RJKDC report](../../../rjkdc-analysis/site/) (Rauh, Jaros,
Kearney, Doran and Cosso) counts it forever. That horizon is the biggest dispute between the two.
]

---
name: part-rows
class: center, middle, inverse

# Part 3: Alternative scenarios

---
name: row-2

# Missing billionaires scenario, part 1: Forbes misses small fortunes

```{r pareto-figs-setup, include=FALSE}
# Billionaires in each $0.5B wealth band from $1B to $5B: the Forbes list (15 April 2026) and the
# Pareto tail fitted above $4.5B. Counts are differences of "number above the cutoff".
cuts <- seq(1, 5, by = 0.5)
band <- function(n) { v <- n[match(cuts, par$threshold_b)]; head(v, -1) - tail(v, -1) }
lab_b <- paste0("$", head(cuts, -1), "-", tail(cuts, -1))
bands <- data.frame(b = factor(lab_b, levels = lab_b),
                    forbes = band(par$n_above_threshold_emp), pareto = band(par$n_above_threshold_proj))
stopifnot(abs(sum(bands$pareto) - (ps$total_count_proj - par$n_above_threshold_emp[par$threshold_b == 5])) < 1e-6)
# Shares of the 617 billionaires a Pareto tail puts above $1B, in both panels, so the left
# panel can stack what Forbes lists (solid) and what it misses (transparent) up to the Pareto bar.
bands$forbes_sh <- bands$forbes / ps$total_count_proj
bands$pareto_sh <- bands$pareto / ps$total_count_proj
bands$miss_sh   <- pmax(bands$pareto_sh - bands$forbes_sh, 0)
ymax <- max(bands$pareto_sh) * 1.15
hfig <- function(y, col, ttl) {
  ggplot(data.frame(b = bands$b, y = y), aes(b, y)) +
    geom_col(fill = col, width = 0.8) + geom_text(aes(label = pct(y)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.6) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, ymax), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0)),
                       labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
    labs(x = "wealth band, $ billion", y = "share of billionaires", title = ttl) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9))
}
```

.pull-left[
```{r pareto-fig-forbes, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.9}
st <- rbind(data.frame(b = bands$b, y = bands$forbes_sh, part = "listed by Forbes"),
            data.frame(b = bands$b, y = bands$miss_sh,   part = "missing"))
st$part <- factor(st$part, levels = c("missing", "listed by Forbes"))
ggplot(st, aes(b, y, fill = part, alpha = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.8, fill = "#d62728") +
  geom_text(data = subset(bands, miss_sh > 0.005), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            aes(b, pareto_sh, label = paste0("+", pct(miss_sh))), vjust = -0.3, size = 3.4, colour = "#d62728") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c("missing" = 0.25, "listed by Forbes" = 1), name = NULL,
                     guide = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = "#d62728"), reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, ymax), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0)),
                     labels = function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")) +
  labs(x = "wealth band, $ billion", y = "share of billionaires", title = "What the Forbes list shows") +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 9), legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.72, 0.78))
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r pareto-fig-typical, fig.width=5, fig.height=2.9}
hfig(bands$pareto_sh, "#1f77b4", "What wealth data usually show")
```
]

Bars are shares of the `r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)` billionaires a Pareto tail puts above $1 billion. **Right:** in wealth and tax
data, top fortunes usually follow a Pareto tail, where each step down holds many more people.
**Left:** Forbes lists only part of each band below $4.5 billion. The pale red is what it misses
(`r pct(bands$miss_sh[1])` of all billionaires in the lowest band alone). Fitted to the Forbes list above $4.5 billion, that shape implies
**`r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)`** billionaires above $1 billion, not `r ps$total_count_emp`.

.small[Method: Pareto extrapolation (BSZ pp.24 to 25, Appendix Figure A4). How it works, in the backup:
[how BSZ detect the gap](#pareto-detail) &middot; [from the gap to `r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)`](#pareto-extrapolation).]

---
name: row-2-revenue

# Missing billionaires scenario, part 2: the revenue

Filling the gap adds `r bn(ps$total_count_proj - ps$total_count_emp, 0)` people but only
$`r bn(ps$total_wealth_proj - ps$total_wealth_emp, 0)` billion: **`r pct(ps$pct_count_increase)`
more people, `r pct(ps$pct_wealth_increase, 1)` more wealth**. The added fortunes are small,
about $`r bn((ps$total_wealth_proj - ps$total_wealth_emp) / (ps$total_count_proj - ps$total_count_emp), 1)` billion each.

The scenario applies those percentages to the 1 July list: `r n0` become `r bn(t5$n_billionaires[2], 0)`
billionaires, and the added wealth is `r pct(ps$pct_wealth_increase, 1)` of $`r bn(W0, 0)` billion
= **$`r bn(dW, 2)` billion**.

| | $ billion |
|---|---:|
| Base scenario revenue (Steps 1 to 3) | `r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1], 2)` |
| + 5% of the added wealth, after a higher `r pct(a_s)` avoidance: 0.05 × `r 1 - a_s` × `r bn(dW, 2)` | + `r bn(add_tax, 2)` |
| − phase-in: the rate rises from 0 to 5% between $1.0 and $1.1 billion; `r pct(ps$fraction_in_phasein, 1)` of the added wealth is in that band | − `r bn(phase, 2)` |
| **= Missing billionaires scenario** | **`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[2], 2)`** |

.small[The ratio b is **research** (estimated from the list). The `r pct(a_s)` avoidance for these less
visible fortunes is <span class="guess">guesswork</span>.
[Report: the missing billionaires scenario](../repro.html#row-2-adding-the-billionaires-forbes-misses).]

---

# Leavers scenario: who may have left

.pull-left[
```{r leavers-tab}
x <- lv
x$name <- tools::toTitleCase(x$name)
x$timing <- ifelse(grepl("^pre", x$timing), "before 1 Jan", "later")
x$wealth <- bn(x$wealth)
x$annual_inctax_loss <- bn(x$annual_inctax_loss, 3)
names(x) <- c("Person", "Left", "Wealth $B", "Inc. tax lost $B/yr")
knitr::kable(x, format = "html", align = "llrr")
```
]

.pull-right[
Assume the four who left **before** 1 January escape the tax, and three more leave later.
Revenue falls to **$`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[3])` billion**; the yearly income tax loss
rises to **$`r bn(-t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[3], 2)` billion**. The **missing + leavers** scenario applies
this and the missing billionaires scenario together.

.highlight-box[
Why so little income tax? SEC filings show the top three pay very little state income tax
relative to their wealth: they rarely sell. Whether any of them has **legally** left is a
<span class="guess">legal judgment</span>, not data.
]
]

---
name: bottom-line

# What the tax collects, and what it costs

```{r bottom-line-tab}
# Present value of the yearly loss over BSZ's 5-year horizon at one rate, 3%, the middle
# of the RJKDC report's 1.5%-4.5% range. The reconciliation page averages over that range
# instead (comparison/R/model.R); the two agree to within $0.01B, checked here.
ann <- function(r, H = 5) (1 - (1 + r)^(-H)) / r
f5  <- ann(0.03)
ls_ <- read.csv("../../../comparison/export/r/loss.csv")
loss <- -t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss
stopifnot(abs(loss[1] * f5 - ls_$pv_5yr[ls_$source_id == "bsz_row1"]) < 0.01,
          abs(loss[3] * f5 - ls_$pv_5yr[ls_$source_id == "bsz_row3"]) < 0.01)
lab <- c("Base", "Missing billionaires", "Leavers", "Missing + leavers")
d <- data.frame(
  Scenario = lab,
  wt = paste0("$", bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue, 1), "B"),
  it = paste0("+$", bn(t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales, 2), "B"),
  l5 = paste0("&minus;$", bn(loss * f5, 2), "B"),
  tot = paste0("$", bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue + t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales - loss * f5, 1), "B"))
en <- read.csv("../../../comparison/export/r/ends.csv")
stopifnot(abs(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] + t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales[1] - loss[1] * f5 -
              en$bsz_model[en$horizon_setting == "own" & en$output == "b"]) < 0.01)
d[1, ] <- paste0("<b>", d[1, ], "</b>")
d$tot[1] <- paste0('<span style="display:inline-block; background:#fff3e0; border:2px solid #e65100; ',
                   'padding:1px 6px; font-weight:700;">$', bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] + t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales[1] - loss[1] * f5, 1),
                   'B<br><span style="font-size:70%; color:#e65100;">MAIN ESTIMATE<sup>1</sup></span></span>')
knitr::kable(d, format = "html", escape = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
  col.names = c("Scenario", "Wealth tax collected<br>(once)",
                "Extra income tax<br>from selling assets<br>(once)",
                "Income tax lost<br>(present value, 5 years)",
                "<b>Total</b>"))
```

.highlight-box[
The income tax loss recurs every year the leavers stay away, so it is a **present value** over BSZ's
horizon of about 5 years at **3% a year**, the middle of the [RJKDC report](../../../rjkdc-analysis/site/)'s 1.5% to 4.5% range (BSZ give no rate).
]

**Change any assumption and watch the main estimate move: [the explorer](../explorer/).**

.small[<sup>1</sup> Not the authors' choice: BSZ's headline is the wealth tax alone, $`r bn(t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1])` billion.
This OPA uses the total as its main estimate because it compares more directly with
[other analyses](../../../index.html), such as the [RJKDC report](../../../rjkdc-analysis/site/)'s net present value.]

name: part-guess

# How far does each guess move the main estimate?

```{r tornado, fig.height=3.0}
keys <- c(avoidance = "Avoidance and evasion", mobility_share = "Share that is leaving",
          avoidance_small = "Avoidance, less visible", sell_share = "Share paid by selling",
          pareto = "Count missing billionaires", leavers = "Aggressive leavers")
# The main estimate: wealth tax + extra income tax - present value of the yearly income
# tax loss over 5 years at 3% (as on the bottom-line slide), for every cell of the grid.
pv5 <- (1 - 1.03^(-5)) / 0.03
grd$net <- grd$wealth_tax_revenue + grd$extra_ca_inctax_sales + grd$annual_ca_inctax_loss * pv5
base <- grd[row1, ]
stopifnot(abs(base$net - (t5$wealth_tax_revenue[1] + t5$extra_ca_inctax_sales[1] +
                          t5$annual_ca_inctax_loss[1] * pv5)) < 1e-9)
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(keys), function(k) {
  keep <- Reduce(`&`, lapply(setdiff(names(keys), k), function(o) abs(grd[[o]] - base[[o]]) < 1e-9))
  data.frame(input = keys[[k]], lo = min(grd$net[keep]), hi = max(grd$net[keep]))
}))
rows$input <- factor(rows$input, levels = rows$input[order(rows$hi - rows$lo)])
guess <- c("Avoidance and evasion", "Share that is leaving", "Avoidance, less visible",
           "Share paid by selling", "Aggressive leavers")   # origin labels: data/inputs.csv
movers <- as.character(rows$input[rows$hi - rows$lo > 1e-9 & rows$input %in% guess])
ggplot(rows, aes(y = input)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lo, xend = hi, yend = input), linewidth = 7, colour = "#1f6fce") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = base$net, colour = "#e65100") +
  labs(x = "main estimate, $ billion (other inputs at the base scenario)", y = NULL)
```

.small[Orange line: the main estimate, $`r bn(base$net)` billion (wealth tax + extra income tax &minus;
income tax lost). Of the five guesses, `r length(movers)` move it on their own:
`r tolower(paste(paste(head(movers, -1), collapse = ", "), tail(movers, 1), sep = " and "))`.
Counting the missing billionaires is research, and only raises it. Every input and its origin:
[report](../repro.html#every-input-by-origin).]

**Try any combination of the guesses: [the explorer](../explorer/).**

# Backup slides

---
name: pareto-detail

# Backup: the Pareto test, in numbers

Forbes may miss smaller fortunes. BSZ test this with one ratio, **b** = the average fortune above
a cutoff ÷ the cutoff. For a Pareto distribution, the usual shape of top wealth, **b** is the same at every cutoff.
The Forbes list the workbook used (15 April 2026):

```{r pareto-tab-backup}
x <- par[par$threshold_b %in% c(10, 4.5, 3, 2, 1), ]
x <- x[order(-x$threshold_b), ]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Cutoff = paste0("$", x$threshold_b, "B"),
  People = x$n_above_threshold_emp,
  Wealth = bn(x$wealth_above_threshold, 0),
  Average = paste0("$", bn(x$wealth_above_threshold / x$n_above_threshold_emp, 2), "B"),
  b = bn(x$pareto_b_emp, 2)),
  format = "html", align = "lrrrr", table.attr = 'style="font-size:80%"',
  col.names = c("Cutoff", "People above it", "Their wealth, $B", "Average fortune", "b"))
```

.highlight-box[
Above $4.5 billion, b stays near `r bn(ps$pareto_b, 2)`. Below it, b climbs to
`r bn(par$pareto_b_emp[par$threshold_b == 1], 1)`: too few people for the wealth above them,
the sign of missing small fortunes. If b stayed at `r bn(ps$pareto_b, 2)` all
the way down, there would be **`r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)`** billionaires above $1 billion,
not `r ps$total_count_emp`.
]

.small[[&larr; Back to the missing billionaires scenario](#row-2)]

---
name: pareto-extrapolation

# Backup: from b to `r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)` billionaires

In a Pareto tail, the number of people above a cutoff $w$ falls like $w^{-a}$. The exponent $a$
and the ratio b describe the same shape: $b = a/(a-1)$, so

$$a = \frac{b}{b-1} = \frac{`r bn(ps$pareto_b, 2)`}{`r bn(ps$pareto_b - 1, 2)`} = `r bn(ps$pareto_a, 2)`$$

BSZ hold b at its value above $4.5 billion and extend the rule down from the
`r par$n_above_threshold_emp[par$threshold_b == 4.5]` billionaires above $4.5 billion:

$$N(w) = `r par$n_above_threshold_emp[par$threshold_b == 4.5]` \times \left(\frac{4.5}{w}\right)^{`r bn(ps$pareto_a, 2)`}, \qquad N(1) = `r bn(ps$total_count_proj, 0)`$$

```{r pareto-extrap-tab}
y <- par[par$threshold_b %in% c(4.5, 2, 1), ]
y <- y[order(-y$threshold_b), ]
stopifnot(abs(par$n_above_threshold_emp[par$threshold_b == 4.5] * 4.5^ps$pareto_a - ps$total_count_proj) < 1e-6)
knitr::kable(data.frame(paste0("$", y$threshold_b, "B"), y$n_above_threshold_emp,
                        bn(y$n_above_threshold_proj, 0)),
  format = "html", align = "lrr", table.attr = 'style="font-size:85%"',
  col.names = c("Cutoff", "Forbes lists", "Pareto tail implies"))
```

.small[The same rule gives the added people's wealth: $`r bn(ps$total_wealth_proj - ps$total_wealth_emp, 0)` billion (BSZ p.25).
[&larr; Back to the scenario](#row-2)]
